lesson.title: Four Equal Directions: sp3 Hybridization
lesson.summary: Four electron domains produce sp3 hybridization, mixing one s orbital and all three p orbitals into four identical tetrahedral hybrid orbitals, the same orbital picture behind methane, ammonia, and water alike.
lesson.body:
Four electron domains around a central atom is the most common situation in introductory chemistry, and it produces sp3 hybridization, the case that started this entire topic. One s orbital mixes with all three p orbitals to build four sp3 hybrid orbitals, each carrying 25 percent s character and 75 percent p character. All four point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, spaced 109.5 degrees apart, matching the tetrahedral electron domain geometry that four domains always produce under VSEPR.

Because sp3 hybridization uses every single valence p orbital in the mix, it leaves nothing behind. Unlike sp and sp2 hybridization, which each leave one or two unhybridized p orbitals available for pi bonding, sp3 hybridization has no leftover p orbitals at all. This is why an sp3 hybridized atom can only ever form sigma bonds, and why any atom drawn with a double or triple bond cannot itself be sp3 hybridized: forming a pi bond requires a pure p orbital that sp3 hybridization has already used up.

Methane, CH4, is the founding example. Carbon has four electron domains, all bonding pairs to hydrogen, so it is sp3 hybridized, and each of its four sp3 orbitals overlaps head on with a hydrogen 1s orbital to form four identical, equivalent C-H sigma bonds at the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5 degrees.

sp3 hybridization does not require all four domains to be bonds, and this is exactly where lone pair repulsion becomes visible at the orbital level. Ammonia's nitrogen has four electron domains, three N-H bonds and one lone pair, all housed in sp3 orbitals, but because one of those orbitals holds a lone pair instead of a bond, the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal rather than tetrahedral, and the extra repulsion from that lone pair compresses the H-N-H angle to about 107 degrees. Water's oxygen carries two lone pairs in two of its four sp3 orbitals, giving a bent molecular shape and an even more compressed H-O-H angle of about 104.5 degrees. In all three molecules, methane, ammonia, and water, the hybridization is identically sp3; only the number of lone pairs occupying those four orbitals changes, and that number is exactly what determines the final shape and angle.

Ethane, C2H6, shows sp3 hybridization applied to a carbon-carbon single bond. Both carbons are sp3 hybridized, each forming three C-H sigma bonds and one C-C sigma bond, all from head on overlap of sp3 orbitals. Because this C-C bond is a single sigma bond with no accompanying pi bond to hold it rigid, the two ends of the ethane molecule can rotate freely around that bond axis without breaking any orbital overlap, a freedom that sp2 and sp hybridized double and triple bonds do not share.

Diamond shows sp3 hybridization extended across an entire solid rather than one small molecule. Every carbon atom in a diamond crystal bonds to four neighboring carbon atoms through sp3 hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally, and because that same bonding pattern repeats from atom to atom without interruption throughout the crystal, diamond forms one continuous three dimensional network instead of separate molecules. That uninterrupted lattice of strong sp3 sigma bonds is a large part of why diamond is exceptionally hard and has such a high melting point compared to molecular solids.
